content: ABC Paint needs a web application to help customers and distributors move from an old paint numbering scheme to a new product line without losing continuity in color selection. Users should be able to translate previous paint numbers, explore available colors, and find suitable products near a chosen color. Authorized staff also need to maintain the colors and product information offered through the application.

We have a few main groups. Customers need to look up old paint numbers, browse the new colors, and see what the closest matching products are so they can keep continuity when they’re choosing paint. Distributors need similar lookup and color-matching access, because they help customers and need to guide them to the right new products. Authorized ABC Paint staff need to add, update, and maintain the color and product information in the system, and they’d also need to see the full data set so they can manage it properly.

The idea is that there should be a clear cross-reference in the app so one legacy paint number points to the current color name and the related product or products. People should be able to search by the old number or by the new name and still land on the same color family or match. We’d want the display to make it obvious what is the legacy reference, what is the current color, and which product or products are associated with it.

Yes, we’d want some of those kept distinct. A legacy paint number is not the same thing as the current color name, and a regional name can be an alternate label rather than a true synonym, so the app should show the relationship instead of collapsing them into one label. There may be cases where different names point to the same color match, but we’d still want the app to preserve which one is the old identifier, which one is the current standard name, and which one is just a local or regional naming variant.

Success would be that they can quickly find the right modern color or product from an old paint number without having to call support or guess. For distributors, it means they can confidently guide customers to the correct replacement or closest match, and for customers it means they can find a suitable option and feel sure it corresponds to what they already know. If the app saves time and reduces confusion during color selection, that would be a good sign it’s working.

We do not have firm targets set yet. I’d say a successful lookup would be one where the user gets a clear match or a clear closest alternative without needing manual help, but the exact usage or conversion goals would need to be defined with the business team.

Right now I know the app will need to rely on our internal product and color data, but I’m not sure yet which systems are the official source of truth versus imported reference files. If the data is incomplete or conflicting, I’d expect the app to show what it can and clearly flag that the match is uncertain rather than inventing an answer, and if a source is unavailable it should fail gracefully and let staff know there’s a data issue. The exact ownership boundary would need to be confirmed with our team.

Good continuity would mean the lookup still feels usable even if one supporting source is slow, with the app showing a clear status instead of timing out silently. If we can still serve cached or previously loaded color and product matches, that would be ideal, but if not, it should give a simple message and avoid showing bad data. For public users, the main thing is that they are not left guessing whether the result is trustworthy.

I don’t have a confirmed schedule yet. My expectation is that the public lookup should be broadly available during normal business hours at first, but whether it becomes 24/7 or rolls out in phases by customer group or distributor group still needs to be decided.

Yes, we should be careful with that. I’d expect search terms and usage logs to be kept only as long as we need them for support, analytics, and improving the matches, and anything that could identify a person should be masked or minimized. The exact retention period and whether we need special treatment for distributor accounts versus public customers would need to be confirmed with compliance and legal.

Yes, that seems likely. My expectation is that distributors may be enabled first or given a slightly different experience during the initial phase, since they are more likely to need the workflow right away and can help validate the results. If one group isn’t live yet, the app should either hide that path or show a clear not-available message rather than exposing a broken lookup.

I don’t have an approved retention period yet. My sense is that distributor-related activity may need to be kept a bit longer for support and account follow-up, while public customer logs should be kept shorter and more anonymized, but that needs confirmation from privacy and records management.

We need to preserve the ability to find the old paint number, understand what it maps to in the new line, and still get to a close color or recommended product without losing the connection people rely on today. Day to day, that means someone who knows an old number should still be able to start there and get a useful answer quickly. Where I expect it to differ is in the presentation and product selection, since the new app should be clearer, more searchable, and probably offer better color browsing than the old catalog ever did.

Yes, absolutely. I would expect the legacy data to be cleaned up so old numbers, color names, and product references are consistent enough for reliable translation and search. Some of the old catalog data is likely messy or duplicated, so we’d need normalization rules before we trust it in the new app.

It should show the nearest matching colors and make it obvious that it’s a substitute rather than the exact original. I’d expect it to rank the options by closeness, probably with the best match first, and include enough information for the user to decide whether the alternative is acceptable.

They should be able to search by name and also narrow results by basic categories like color family and product type. I’d expect the filters to be simple and fast, not overly technical, so customers and distributors can get to a shortlist without needing to know the full catalog structure.

Side by side comparison would be useful, especially when the choices are close and people need to see small differences. A ranked shortlist alone may be enough for a quick lookup, but for real selection work I’d expect the app to let them compare a few candidates at once.

The main constraint is that both customers and distributors may depend on it during normal business hours, so it needs to be reliable and easy to access from the web without special setup. I’d also want to avoid a rollout that disrupts existing ways of finding colors, so there should be a controlled transition and enough support for staff while people learn the new catalog. If there are hosting or uptime targets, I’d need to verify those with the team.

It should be available essentially all the time during business hours, because people may be using it while they’re helping customers or placing orders. Short maintenance windows outside business hours would probably be acceptable, but unexpected downtime during the day would be a problem, especially if it blocks color lookups or product matching.

Yes, there would likely be branding rules so the app matches ABC Paint’s corporate look and uses product and color names consistently with approved usage. I would also expect basic accessibility support, because some users may rely on screen readers or keyboard navigation. On trademark or naming restrictions, I’d need to check the company’s legal and marketing guidance to be sure of the exact rules.

It should still return the nearest valid options and clearly explain that there isn’t an exact one-to-one replacement. I’d want the app to preserve the old number in the search or lookup result, then guide the user to the closest current colors or products so they can continue without losing the reference.

Staff access should be controlled with normal company login credentials, and maintenance functions should be limited to authorized users only. Different roles would probably matter, because not everyone should be able to edit the catalog or change product mappings, and higher-risk changes may need extra approval or at least a stricter permission level. I’d need to confirm the exact authentication standard with IT.

I’d expect a small admin or catalog-management group to handle that work, probably with one or two supervisors in the mix. Regular staff should not be changing mappings, and anything that affects how old numbers translate to new products should be restricted to a higher permission level. For especially sensitive updates, like bulk changes or removing a widely used color, I’d want some kind of review or approval step.

We’d want the lookup to fail gracefully rather than just stop working. If the service is slow, it should keep the user informed and still return whatever data it can; if it’s temporarily unavailable, a clear message and possibly a fallback to the last known catalog data would be better than a blank screen. For exact uptime and recovery targets, I’d need to confirm what the business wants, but the key thing is not losing the ability to search.

Yes, it should make the closest matches very obvious and show a short explanation of why they’re being suggested. If there are multiple near matches, narrowing by product line, finish, or color family would help a lot, and the app should avoid presenting a long confusing list. The goal is to help someone get to a usable choice quickly, especially when they started from an old number.

The comparison should show the color names, the old and new numbers if available, the product line, and any note about how close the match is. It would also help to show a visual swatch and maybe a short difference summary so the user can tell them apart at a glance. I think comparing a small set at once, like three to five colors, is reasonable, but I’d verify the exact limit with the team.

We’d definitely need training for staff so they understand how to use the new lookup and maintenance functions, especially the mapping between old and new numbers. A temporary period where both old and new catalog access work side by side would be very helpful so customers and distributors can adjust without disruption. We’d also want some customer-facing help, like quick guides or support from distributors, during the first part of the rollout.

Yes, we should stick to approved product and color names wherever possible, especially anything customer-facing. Abbreviations or aliases might be okay internally or as search aids, but they shouldn’t replace the official names in the main display unless marketing signs off. If there’s any new naming, renaming, or legacy-number label that could be legally sensitive or customer-visible, that would need review before it goes live.

It should keep the old number visible throughout the flow and clearly show the matched new product or color alongside it. After the lookup, the app should offer a simple path to browse nearby or related colors from that result, so they can explore without having to start over. I’d also keep the original reference in the breadcrumb or result header so they always know where they came from.

Users should always see the latest approved mapping by default, since that’s the current source of truth. If a mapping changed after a release, it would be useful to show some indication that the result was updated, at least for staff and maybe in a simple “recently changed” note for users. I don’t think we’d want to expose every prior match in the normal customer view unless there’s a specific business reason.

We should define that now, at least at a high level. My expectation is that old-number lookup and browsing new colors should be open to customers and distributors, while maintaining the mappings and product data should be limited to authorized staff. If there are finer-grained rules later, we can capture them, but the basic access split should be decided now.

Staff should see the full change history, including the previous mappings, who made each change, and when it happened, so they can audit it properly. For other users, a simpler “updated recently” indicator is enough and should not expose the full history. If we need to hide user names for privacy or policy reasons, that would be something to confirm with the team, but the audit trail itself should exist.

Yes, I’d want only approved changes in the main audit trail, since that’s what matters operationally. Superseded mappings should remain visible as history, even if they’re no longer active, but deleted entries might need a separate treatment depending on why they were removed. I’d expect the history to go back as far as we have reliable records for, but if older data is incomplete, we should clearly mark that rather than pretending it’s complete.

Changes should not go live the moment someone edits them unless that person has explicit release rights. In general, I’d expect an authorized staff member to make the update, then a reviewer or approver confirms it, and only after that it becomes active in the catalog. If a release is already in progress, I’d rather queue the change for the next release window unless it’s a critical correction that needs immediate attention.

We should record it as a confirmed rule now. The basic access model is clear enough: customers and distributors can look up and browse, while only authorized staff can maintain mappings and product data.

A critical correction should be something that would clearly mislead users or cause the wrong product to be selected if we waited, like a bad color match, an incorrect old-number translation, or a product record that’s simply wrong or missing. I’d also include anything that affects safety, legal labeling, or a known high-volume customer order issue. Routine wording changes or preference tweaks should definitely wait for the next release.

Our internal product and color data should be treated as authoritative. If an imported reference file conflicts and the system can’t resolve it confidently, it should flag the item for staff review instead of guessing. I’d want the conflicting import to be held back or marked inactive until someone confirms the correct mapping.

The practical limit should be whatever still lets someone compare them comfortably on a normal laptop screen without scrolling through a huge table. I’d expect that to be a small handful, maybe around five to seven colors at once, because once you add names, numbers, swatches, and notes, it gets crowded fast. If they want to compare more than that, the app should let them narrow the list or compare in batches.

They should be able to correct the mapping and activate it if they have the right authority, leave it inactive if they’re not ready to publish, or reject it entirely if the source is bad. I’d expect some staff roles to only review or comment, not edit or activate, especially for higher-risk data like core color mappings. If the conflict is tied to a release issue or a master record, it should probably be restricted to a smaller approval group.

It should come down to role and data sensitivity. People with a basic maintenance or review role can look and comment, but only a limited set of trusted staff should be able to edit mappings or activate anything that affects the master record or a release. If it’s tied to a release issue, I’d want it locked down even further so only the release approver or data owner can make the final call.

Yes, there should be branding and accessibility rules, but I don’t have the full standards document in front of me. At minimum, the catalog should use approved ABC Paint logo treatment, maintain readable contrast, and avoid layouts that make swatches or labels hard to interpret. Product and color names should be shown exactly as approved, and if legal or marketing restrictions apply, the app should not improvise alternate names or display text.

Yes, there can be cases where a specific product or color entry needs its branding elements or approved name adjusted or suppressed, but only if legal, marketing, or accessibility has signed off. In those cases, I’d expect the change to be limited to that affected entry rather than the whole catalog. If the issue is unresolved, the safer choice is to hide or flag the entry instead of publishing something potentially noncompliant.

Once sign-off is obtained, I’d expect the entry to be updated in place and then unhidden or reactivated, but still go through a quick review or approval step before it becomes visible again. That keeps the history intact while making sure the final published version is the one that was actually approved. If the change is minor and already preapproved in the workflow, that review could be lightweight, but I wouldn’t skip validation entirely.
